old_entry.title: Dune II
old_entry.summary: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty (titled Dune II: Battle for Arrakis in Europe and Dune: The Battle for Arrakis in North America for the Mega Drive/Genesis port, respectively) is a 1992 real-time strategy game developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Games.
body: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty (titled Dune II: Battle for Arrakis in Europe and Dune: The Battle for Arrakis in North America for the Mega Drive/Genesis port, respectively) is a 1992 real-time strategy game developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Games. It serves as the sequel to Dune (a more traditional adventure game), which came out earlier that same year.

While not the first real-time strategy (RTS) video game, Dune II established the format that would be followed for years to come. As such, Dune II is the archetypal real-time strategy game. Striking a balance between complexity and innovation, it was a huge success and laid the foundation for Age of Empires, Warcraft, Westwood Studios' subsequent strategy game Command & Conquer, and many other RTS games that followed.

old_entry.title: Alone in the Dark
old_entry.summary: Alone in the Dark is a 1992 survival horror video game designed by Frédérick Raynal.
body: Alone in the Dark is a 1992 survival horror video game designed by Frédérick Raynal. Developed and published by Infogrames in 1992 for MS-DOS, the game was eventually ported to Mac OS, the PC-98, the FM Towns, the 3DO, RISC OS, and iOS. Alone in the Dark is set in 1920s Louisiana and challenges the player to escape a haunted mansion. To advance, the player must solve puzzles while banishing, slaying, or eluding various ghosts and monsters. The player can collect and use weapons, manage a weight-based inventory system, and explore a partially nonlinear map.

Raynal was motivated to create Alone in the Dark due to his interest in 3D animation and his fondness for horror films. The storyline was inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft and the work of directors like Dario Argento and George A. Romero. Raynal's programming team worked to convey much of this story via key texts scattered about the game's environment. To overcome technical limitations, the production team also employed a fixed camera angle system to dramatically frame the movement of three-dimensional characters on top of two-dimensional background images.

Upon its release, Alone in the Dark received acclaim, with critics applauding its unsettling atmosphere, effective soundtrack, and technical inventiveness. The game also won several industry awards and is regularly included in lists of the best video games ever made. Often identified as the first 3D survival horror game, Alone in the Dark strongly influenced the production of Capcom's Resident Evil (1996), and it also spawned a series of follow-up games and two films. A reimagining of the original game, published by THQ Nordic, was released on 20 March 2024.

old_entry.title: Ecco the Dolphin
old_entry.summary: Ecco the Dolphin is an action-adventure game developed by Ed Annunziata and Novotrade International and published by Sega for the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1992.
body: Ecco the Dolphin is an action-adventure game developed by Ed Annunziata and Novotrade International and published by Sega for the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1992. Versions for the Sega CD, Master System, and Game Gear were released the following years. It is the first installment in the Ecco the Dolphin video game franchise. The player character is a bottlenose dolphin who travels through time to combat hostile extraterrestrials in Earth's oceans and on an alien spacecraft.

Ecco the Dolphin received favourable reviews and became a bestseller on the Genesis. It has been re-released several times, including on the Nintendo Virtual Console, Xbox Live Arcade, Steam, iOS, Nintendo 3DS, and the Nintendo Classics service. A sequel, Ecco: The Tides of Time, was released in 1994.

old_entry.title: Contra III: The Alien Wars
old_entry.summary: Contra III: The Alien Wars is a 1992 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
body: Contra III: The Alien Wars is a 1992 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third home console entry in the Contra series after Contra (1988) and Super C (1990) for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). In PAL regions, it was retitled Super Probotector: Alien Rebels and the player characters were replaced with robots. The player is tasked with fighting off an alien invasion of Earth across six stages. Four stages feature side-scrolling action traditional to the series while two are presented from an overhead perspective. It is the first Contra title to have been directed by Nobuya Nakazato who later directed other games in the series. He designed Contra III to feature more comical elements, a more cinematic soundtrack, and tighter stage design than its predecessors.

Contra III received positive reviews, with critics praising its arcade quality derived from its sound and visual design. It has been called one of the best Contra games in retrospective reviews and is considered one of the greatest video games of all time. It was ported to the Game Boy as Contra: The Alien Wars (1994) by Factor 5 where it received positive reviews for its Super Game Boy enhancements. Konami also released a Game Boy Advance port titled Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (2002) which received more critical reviews for removing features in the original. The Super NES version was rereleased several times including the Super NES Classic Edition, Contra Anniversary Collection, and various online distribution services.

old_entry.title: Ultima VII: The Black Gate
old_entry.summary: Ultima VII: The Black Gate is the seventh installment of the Ultima series of role-playing video games.
body: Ultima VII: The Black Gate is the seventh installment of the Ultima series of role-playing video games. It was published in April 1992 for MS-DOS by Origin Systems. The player returns as The Avatar, a would-be paragon of moral virtue who faces down many dangers and deceptions in order to cleanse the medieval fantasy world of Britannia of assorted plots and schemes, monster infestations, and the undermining of crown authority. A Super NES conversion was released in 1994.

The Black Gate was critically acclaimed and commercially successful, being widely lauded as a high point in the series and is also regarded as one of the best video games ever created. In an interview with GameSpot, Richard Garriott stated that Ultima VII "was the most masterfully executed of the Ultima series". He has also often stated that the game was, along with Ultima IV, his own favorite installment overall.

old_entry.title: Mario Paint
old_entry.subtitle: Mario Paint Turns the Super Famicom into a Creative Tool
old_entry.summary: On July 14, 1992 Nintendo released Mario Paint for Super Famicom in Japan.
body: On July 14, 1992 Nintendo released Mario Paint for Super Famicom in Japan. Sold with a mouse, the software shifts the console from consumption toward production: players can draw, animate, compose short musical sequences and play with the interface tools themselves. Mario and Nintendo's visual language make functions resembling a small multimedia workshop approachable. Mario Paint matters because it shows how a peripheral and an interface designed together can change the fundamental question from what the player should do to what the player can create.

The drawing board offers 15 colours and 75 patterns, with pens, an airbrush, fills, lines, rectangles and circles. Parts of a picture can be copied, pasted, moved or flipped. Animation Land uses the same tools to build animations of four, six or nine frames, and the mouse can record a path for an animated object to follow. A separate stamp editor lets users alter existing stamps or draw their own.

The music composer represents sounds with familiar icons: Mario's head plays piano, a Power Star rings like a bell, and a Game Boy produces a pulse wave. Notes are placed on a treble clef. Compositions use common or triple time, with no sharps or flats and no more than three notes on a beat. Finished pieces can accompany animations and the colouring book.

The title screen and Gnat Attack help players learn the SNES Mouse. Clicking the letters and scenery on the title screen triggers hidden animations. In Gnat Attack, the player swats 100 insects before fighting King Watinga. Its three levels repeat with faster enemies, turning precise pointing into a game of its own.

original_body: On July 14, 1992 Nintendo released Mario Paint for Super Famicom in Japan. Sold with a mouse, the software shifts the console from consumption toward production: players can draw, animate, compose short musical sequences and play with the interface tools themselves. Mario and Nintendo's visual language make functions resembling a small multimedia workshop approachable. Mario Paint matters because it shows how a peripheral and an interface designed together can change the fundamental question from what the player should do to what the player can create.

Drawing, selecting and dragging require continuous pointing instead of a traditional pad, so the peripheral does more than add convenience: it enables different activities on the television. Readability is part of the mechanic. Visual or audio signals, response time and information hierarchy must reveal enough to support a decision without removing uncertainty. When the interface works, players do not merely receive data: they build a mental model of the situation and learn where to place their attention. This solution matters beyond one title, because many conventions of the medium emerged precisely from the need to make new complexity understandable without slowing the action.

Visual tools coexist with simple animation and an icon-based composer, making the console feel like a small multimedia studio rather than a machine dedicated to one genre. The mechanic does not live in isolation: it changes the value of space, time and resources, forcing players to build priorities while the situation changes. That relationship between a local decision and the rhythm of the whole play session is what makes the system memorable. The mouse changes the console's vocabulary
Drawing, animation and music share the same box
Even the interface becomes a toy

1.heading: Drawing and animation
1.text: The drawing board offers 15 colours and 75 patterns, with pens, an airbrush, fills, lines, rectangles and circles. Parts of a picture can be copied, pasted, moved or flipped. Animation Land uses the same tools to build animations of four, six or nine frames, and the mouse can record a path for an animated object to follow. A separate stamp editor lets users alter existing stamps or draw their own.

source_paragraphs.text: The drawing board is where original paintings can be created. A user can choose from 15 colors and 75 patterns. After choosing, the user can draw with a pen (small, medium, or large) and airbrush;  fill in a closed area the selected texture with the "paint brush" tool; and create perfectly straight lines, rectangles, and circles that is the color or pattern selected (either fully colored-in, with just an outline, or with a spray-canned outline). Parts of a drawing can be copied, pasted, and moved to other areas, rotated vertically and horizontally, or erased via pens of six various sizes. An entire painting can also be erased via nine unique visual effects. Animation Land involves the use of the drawing board's tools for creating four, six, and/or nine-frame animations. Elements of one frame can be copied to others for smooth animations to be created. If a character is being animated, the animation box can be set on a background and move throughout it in a "path" recorded by using the mouse in the "path lever" feature.

In the animation and drawing features, stamps can be added to each painting and frame, with 120 existing stamps included in the software. There is a stamp editor that allows the user to create new stamps or edit existing ones via a large tile grid, with the same 15 colors from the drawing board usable in the stamp editor. Up to 15 user-made stamps can be saved to a "personal stamp database". There are also text stamps, such as English, Hiragana, Katakana, and Kanji characters, that can be added and changed in size and color.

2.heading: Music written with icons
2.text: The music composer represents sounds with familiar icons: Mario's head plays piano, a Power Star rings like a bell, and a Game Boy produces a pulse wave. Notes are placed on a treble clef. Compositions use common or triple time, with no sharps or flats and no more than three notes on a beat. Finished pieces can accompany animations and the colouring book.

source_paragraphs.text: The music composer allows users to write pieces either in common time or triple time. There are 15 instruments samples to use that are notated with different icons, including eight melodic sounds (a piano represented by Mario's head, a bell sound represented by a Power Star, a trumpet represented by a Fire Flower, a pulse wave represented by the Game Boy, a horn section sample represented by a goose, a guitar sound represented by an airliner, and an organ represented by a car), three percussion sounds (a bass drum represented by a Super Mushroom, a woodblock represented by a ship, and a bass pluck represented by a heart), and five sound effects (Yoshi's zip, a dog bark, a cat meow, a pig oink, and a baby hiccup). The icons are added to a treble clef. Notes that can be added are limited to a range from the B below middle C to high G. Since no flats or sharps can be added, pieces are restricted to notes of the C major/A minor scale. Other limitations include composing only in quarter notes, a maximum number of three notes on a beat, and a maximum number of measures a song can last (24 bars for 44 songs, and 32 bars for 34 songs). Pieces made in the composition tool can be played in the animation and coloring book modes.

3.heading: Learning the mouse through play
3.text: The title screen and Gnat Attack help players learn the SNES Mouse. Clicking the letters and scenery on the title screen triggers hidden animations. In Gnat Attack, the player swats 100 insects before fighting King Watinga. Its three levels repeat with faster enemies, turning precise pointing into a game of its own.

source_paragraphs.text: According to the manual, two parts of Mario Paint are meant to familiarize the user with the SNES Mouse: the title screen, where users can click on each letter in the logo and each element on the screen to prompt a respective Easter egg; and a fly-swatting minigame, "Gnat Attack", where the player must swat 100 insects before fighting a boss named King Watinga. The minigame has three levels, and after they are completed, the game starts over with the enemies swarming in and attacking at faster speed. Content creation features of the program include a drawing board, a coloring book, an animation tool (called "Animation Land"), and a music composer. Collages can be saved at a time in the program to be loaded at later usage of the software or recorded to VCR. In the coloring book, the user can color-in and edit four pre-made black-and-white drawings, including one featuring Yoshi and Mario, another featuring various animals, a greeting card, and an underwater scene.

The Recca ship can carry five different main weapons, each with advantages and disadvantages. Weapon icons dropped by enemies equip or upgrade them. Five kinds of sub-weapon supply satellite-like options that shoot in different directions. Clearing normal mode unlocks a harder second loop with seven rearranged stages.

When the player stops firing the main weapon briefly, an energy shield charges in front of the ship. It absorbs ordinary enemy projectiles and can be launched to destroy enemies within its blast radius. Firing continuously and preparing this defence therefore require different timings.

Score Attack asks the player to earn as many points as possible in two minutes. Time Attack instead measures how quickly two stages can be completed within five minutes. body: On July 24, 1992 Technosoft released Thunder Force IV for Mega Drive in Japan. The horizontal shooter expands the series' scale with stages taller than the screen, multiple scrolling layers and an arsenal that can be switched during play. The player must read ship position, terrain and available weapons at the same time while the soundtrack pushes the hardware toward an aggressive sonic identity. Its reputation comes from the meeting of technique and control: the console appears to show more than the screen can contain, yet the action remains readable.

Thunder Force IV is a horizontal shoot 'em up. The story takes place two years after the events of Thunder Force III. The player takes on the role of a fighter pilot to battle the Orn Empire, which is plotting the extinction of the human race. The first four stages can be selected in any order. There are ten stages total. They scroll horizontally automatically, and the player can also explore up and down to scroll the screen vertically and reveal a larger playing field. The player can change the speed of their ship at any time for easier maneuverability. Scrolling up and down will reveal different waves of enemies the player can shoot down, as well as hidden power-ups. At the end of each stage is a boss, and sometimes there are bosses mid-stage.

Some enemies will drop power-ups that if picked up by the player will arm the ship with new weaponry, including a variety of missiles and lasers that fire in different patterns. Each weapon has advantages and drawbacks, and is more or less effective depending on the battle situation the player finds themselves in. The player can hold multiple weapons and cycle through them at will. Other power-ups include shields and satellite ships that revolve around their ship and multiply their firepower. Half-way through the game, the player gains a powerful "Thunder Sword" attack which deals massive damage to enemies. It requires that the player have two satellite ships.

The sound team, led by Naosuke Arai, were fans of heavy metal and tried to create the sound of an electric guitar using the Mega Drive's FM synthesizer. After encountering difficulties, they used the system's distortion sound effects to achieve the result. The rest of the development team had previously worked on the Mega Drive conversion of Devil's Crush.

old_entry.title: Super Mario Kart
old_entry.subtitle: Racing Became a Language for Playing Together
old_entry.summary: Nintendo released Super Mario Kart in Japan for the Super Famicom on August 27, 1992.
body: Nintendo released Super Mario Kart in Japan for the Super Famicom on August 27, 1992. The project began with a very specific technical problem: create an F-Zero-like racing game for two players even though the console could not sustain two high-speed views of the same kind. The solution changed the entire design. Karts became slower, tracks more compact and Mode 7 perspective easier to read in split screen. Mario entered only later, because his world allowed bananas, shells and familiar characters to become an immediate grammar. From that compromise emerged one of Nintendo's most influential series, able to make competition accessible without removing racing lines, drifting, track memory and rivalry.

Super Mario Kart does not begin with Mario. Hideki Konno recalls that Shigeru Miyamoto gave the team a technical assignment: make something like F-Zero for two players. Split screen made the original model's long straights and extreme speed impractical. The team slowed the action, compacted the tracks and searched for vehicles that remained readable in a smaller viewport. A hardware limitation therefore changed the shape of the circuit itself. Before shells and characters, Mario Kart emerged from a display and local-multiplayer problem. It is an unusually clear example of design growing directly from the characteristics of available hardware.

The Super Nintendo can rotate and scale a graphic plane with Mode 7, and Super Mario Kart uses that ability to turn a two-dimensional surface into a track perceived in perspective. The circuit remains technically flat, but the camera and kart sprites produce a convincing sense of depth. This solution influences level design: tracks must be compact, recognizable from above and clear enough to work in split screen. The technology is therefore more than a visual effect. It determines curves, width, obstacles and the way players anticipate what will happen a few seconds later.

In a conventional race, the fastest driver tends to pull away and make the result predictable. Super Mario Kart introduces items that let players interfere directly with one another: shells, banana peels and power-ups repeatedly reshape the gaps between racers. Their value lies not only in chaos but in creating decisions between driving and attacking. Keeping an item, using it defensively or throwing it immediately changes the relationship with other drivers. Competition becomes a conversation made of trajectories and mischief. This principle will make the series approachable without turning it into a game where skill no longer matters.

old_entry.title: Dragon Quest V
old_entry.summary: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride, known in Europe as Dragon Quest: The Hand of the Heavenly Bride and in Japan as Dragon Quest V: Bride of Heaven, is a 1992 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Super Famicom.
body: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride, known in Europe as Dragon Quest: The Hand of the Heavenly Bride and in Japan as Dragon Quest V: Bride of Heaven, is a 1992 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Super Famicom. The fifth main installment in the Dragon Quest series, the game was the first title in the franchise to not be initially localized in North America due to programming issues.

It later had an enhanced remake only in Japan for the PlayStation 2 in 2004. The remake was developed by ArtePiazza and Matrix Software. Another remake was made for the Nintendo DS, which was released in Japan in July 2008 and worldwide in February 2009; this marks the first time the game had officially released in English. In addition, ports for Android and iOS were released in Japan in December 2014, and worldwide the following month.

The game takes place over roughly thirty years of the main character's life, from when he is born through to when he gets married and has a family. The title introduced a gameplay dynamic in which monsters from random encounters may offer to join the player's party. This concept was used in later Dragon Quest games, as well as in the Dragon Quest Monsters series as the primary way to form a party. The game's monster-collecting concept had been used before in the Megami Tensei series and appeared in many later franchises such as Pokémon, Digimon and Dokapon. In turn, the concept of collecting everything in a game, in the form of achievements or similar rewards, has since become a common trend in video games. Dragon Quest V has also been credited as the first known video game to feature a playable pregnancy, a concept that has since appeared in later games such as Story of Seasons, The Sims 2 and Fable II. In 2019, an animated film adaptation, Dragon Quest: Your Story, was released in Japan. The film was later released digitally for other regions through Netflix.

old_entry.title: Mortal Kombat
old_entry.subtitle: Fighting Finds Another Face
old_entry.summary: On October 8, 1992, Mortal Kombat debuted in U.S. arcades.
body: On October 8, 1992, Mortal Kombat debuted in U.S. arcades. Midway entrusted Ed Boon, John Tobias and a very small team with a fighting game that sought an identity different from that of already established competitors. The most visible solution was the use of digitized actors, but its importance did not end with the photographic look. Mortal Kombat builds recognizable characters, rivalries and rituals, makes blocking a dedicated command and turns the end of a match into a separate spectacle through Fatalities. Its success quickly carries the game out of the arcade and into a broader public debate about violence in video games. Even before its sequels, the 1992 title therefore shows how visual technology, mechanics and marketing can merge into an immediately identifiable cultural form.

Digitization transfers the poses and movements of real performers onto the screen. It does not remove artistic work: those images have to be selected, adapted and organized so that they become readable actions. John Tobias has linked the game's rougher tone directly to this technique. The contrast with impossible powers and fantastical environments produces a distinctive quality. The bodies seem to come from the everyday world, while what they do belongs to another logic. Credibility is not the same as absolute realism. It comes from the meeting between recognizable presence and deliberate exaggeration. This solution helps distinguish Mortal Kombat at a glance, but it truly works when the recorded gesture also becomes a useful signal for the person fighting.

Mortal Kombat uses an 8-directional joystick and 5 buttons, including 2 punch and 2 kick buttons, each further differentiated between high and low. Attacks can vary depending on the player's distance from the opponent. All player characters have a shared set of attacks performed by holding the joystick in various directions, such as a leg sweep and an uppercut. The latter attack knocks the enemy high into the air and causes much damage. Most special moves were performed by tapping the joystick, sometimes ending with a button press. Unlike previous one-on-one fighting games, few moves require circular joystick movement. The game's blocking system also distinguished itself from other fighting games, as characters take a small amount of damage from regular moves while blocking. However, the dedicated block button allows users to defend against attacks without retreating. Blocking characters lose very little ground when struck, thus making counterattacks much easier after a successful block.

The game takes place in Earthrealm, where a tournament is being held on Shang Tsung's Island, on which seven of its locations serve as stages in the game. The introduction to Mortal Kombat explains that Shang Tsung was banished to Earthrealm 500 years ago and, with the help of the monstrous Goro, seized control of the Mortal Kombat tournament in an attempt to doom the realm. For 500 years straight, Goro has been undefeated in the tournament and has won nine consecutive tournaments. If Goro wins again, Shao Kahn, Emperor of Outworld, will be allowed to take Earthrealm. To prevent this, a new generation of warriors must challenge Goro.

Mortal Kombat further introduced the concept of "juggling", knocking an opponent into the air and following up with a combination of attacks while the enemy is still airborne and defenseless. The idea became so popular that it spread to many other games. Another of the game's innovations was the Fatality, a finishing move performed against a defeated opponent to execute them in a gruesome fashion.

To give the tournament a creature that could not be achieved simply by filming an actor, the team built Goro as an articulated puppet and digitized its poses. The solution brings a logic close to practical special effects into the video game: construct a physical object, animate it frame by frame and turn that material into sprites usable by arcade hardware. John Tobias has described this process as part of the search for visually distinct characters. Goro is not merely a larger boss. His four arms immediately communicate a different hierarchy from the human fighters and reinforce the idea that the tournament belongs to a world that exceeds the realism of digitized actors. Different techniques therefore coexist on the same screen in support of a single fiction.

When Mortal Kombat reaches home consoles in 1993, its violence becomes part of a public discussion that extends beyond the arcade audience. U.S. Senate hearings on violent video games cited Mortal Kombat alongside other titles and contributed to the climate that led the American industry to create the ESRB in 1994. It is important to distinguish this cultural consequence from the date of the original arcade game: October 8, 1992 marks the game's debut, while the political controversy develops above all after its home release. The episode shows how a visual language designed to attract attention in an arcade can take on a different meaning when it enters homes, mass marketing and debate about content ratings.

editorial_features.title: Who gets to rate a game?
editorial_features.summary: From a hearing to a label.
body: On 9 December 1993, senators Joseph Lieberman and Herb Kohl held a joint hearing about violent video games and information for parents. The Senate committee's later report records testimony from educators and other witnesses, as well as representatives including Nintendo's Howard Lincoln and Sega's Bill White. It says industry representatives committed to creating a rating system for the 1994 holidays. The document preserves its concerns and commitments. It does not, by recording them, establish that the witnesses' claims about violence were proven.

A second joint hearing on 4 March 1994 examined the industry's preliminary proposal. According to the committee report, a central question was how the system could demonstrate independence and credibility. Retail representatives also supported participating in a future scheme. The practical issue extended beyond deciding which words belonged on a box: publishers and shops would have to recognise the same process. This record helps distinguish a proposal discussed under political pressure from a government agency directly classifying every game offered for sale in the United States.

The ESRB's own chronology dates its foundation to 1994, under the Interactive Digital Software Association. It records five rating categories and seventeen content descriptors at the system's announcement. These were two different kinds of information: an age category and details about the material inside. The organisation's account is useful for following its published structure, while remaining its own institutional history. It should not stand in for evidence that every parent interpreted a label alike, or that the system resolved every disagreement over a game's content.

The labels and their administration changed after that first announcement. ESRB records an advertising code in 1995, the replacement of Kids to Adults with Everyone in 1998, and an Advertising Review Council in 2000. Its chronology also places a sanctions system in 2000, including points, fines and corrective action. Rating a product and policing how companies market it had become related responsibilities. Looking at the dates separately prevents the familiar present-day symbols from being projected backwards as though the whole scheme had arrived fully formed.

original.old_body: Mortal Kombat assigns blocking to a dedicated command. It is a concrete difference from fighting games in which defense depends mainly on moving backward. The player has to incorporate a specific gesture into their rhythm, deciding when to interrupt offense and protect themselves. Characters share part of the basic vocabulary, while special moves characterize their possibilities. This balance helps with initial orientation: changing fighter does not mean learning every action again from the beginning. At the same time, recognizing an opponent's technique remains necessary. The personality of the system emerges from this combination of familiarity and difference. Combat is not merely a showcase for spectacular effects; it requires managing distance, waiting and vulnerability within a precise grammar.
original.heading: Five buttons, shared attacks and blocking
original.body: Mortal Kombat uses an 8-directional joystick and 5 buttons, including 2 punch and 2 kick buttons, each further differentiated between high and low. Attacks can vary depending on the player's distance from the opponent. All player characters have a shared set of attacks performed by holding the joystick in various directions, such as a leg sweep and an uppercut. The latter attack knocks the enemy high into the air and causes much damage. Most special moves were performed by tapping the joystick, sometimes ending with a button press. Unlike previous one-on-one fighting games, few moves require circular joystick movement. The game's blocking system also distinguished itself from other fighting games, as characters take a small amount of damage from regular moves while blocking. However, the dedicated block button allows users to defend against attacks without retreating. Blocking characters lose very little ground when struck, thus making counterattacks much easier after a successful block.

original.old_body: Liu Kang, Raiden, Sonya, Johnny Cage, Scorpion and Sub-Zero do not arrive on screen with the same kind of promise. Martial arts, cinema, supernatural forces and personal rivalries coexist within the tournament. A few distinctive elements are enough to suggest that each fighter also exists beyond the round. John Tobias has described work on the characters' origins and motivations as a fundamental part of their construction. The brevity of the arcade format forces a great deal into very little space: a name, a pose and a move have to be memorable. The world is therefore anticipated through fragments. The player does not yet know everything, but there are enough clues to want to distinguish one character from another even when that character is not the one being used to win.

original.heading: Shang Tsung, Goro and the tournament
original.body: The game takes place in Earthrealm, where a tournament is being held on Shang Tsung's Island, on which seven of its locations serve as stages in the game. The introduction to Mortal Kombat explains that Shang Tsung was banished to Earthrealm 500 years ago and, with the help of the monstrous Goro, seized control of the Mortal Kombat tournament in an attempt to doom the realm. For 500 years straight, Goro has been undefeated in the tournament and has won nine consecutive tournaments. If Goro wins again, Shao Kahn, Emperor of Outworld, will be allowed to take Earthrealm. To prevent this, a new generation of warriors must challenge Goro.

original.old_body: The Fatality comes after the match has already been decided. Precisely for this reason it changes the meaning of victory: instead of merely communicating a result, it grants a brief ritual space in which the player can perform a sequence and turn the conclusion into spectacle. John Tobias has recalled how the idea of finishing moves developed alongside the project's exaggerated tone. Their power depends not only on violence, but on temporal structure. They require knowledge, distance and precision at a moment when there is no longer an active opponent to overcome. The arcade audience can therefore recognize skill and secret knowledge in the same gesture. Mortal Kombat makes the post-fight memorable and creates a format that would become inseparable from the series' identity.

original.heading: Juggling and Fatalities
original.body: Mortal Kombat further introduced the concept of "juggling", knocking an opponent into the air and following up with a combination of attacks while the enemy is still airborne and defenseless. The idea became so popular that it spread to many other games. Another of the game's innovations was the Fatality, a finishing move performed against a defeated opponent to execute them in a gruesome fashion.

editorial_features.title: Who gets to rate a game?
editorial_features.summary: From a hearing to a label.
body: On 9 December 1993, senators Joseph Lieberman and Herb Kohl held a joint hearing about violent video games and information for parents. The Senate committee's later report records testimony from educators and other witnesses, as well as representatives including Nintendo's Howard Lincoln and Sega's Bill White. It says industry representatives committed to creating a rating system for the 1994 holidays. The document preserves its concerns and commitments. It does not, by recording them, establish that the witnesses' claims about violence were proven.

A second joint hearing on 4 March 1994 examined the industry's preliminary proposal. According to the committee report, a central question was how the system could demonstrate independence and credibility. Retail representatives also supported participating in a future scheme. The practical issue extended beyond deciding which words belonged on a box: publishers and shops would have to recognise the same process. This record helps distinguish a proposal discussed under political pressure from a government agency directly classifying every game offered for sale in the United States.

The ESRB's own chronology dates its foundation to 1994, under the Interactive Digital Software Association. It records five rating categories and seventeen content descriptors at the system's announcement. These were two different kinds of information: an age category and details about the material inside. The organisation's account is useful for following its published structure, while remaining its own institutional history. It should not stand in for evidence that every parent interpreted a label alike, or that the system resolved every disagreement over a game's content.

The labels and their administration changed after that first announcement. ESRB records an advertising code in 1995, the replacement of Kids to Adults with Everyone in 1998, and an Advertising Review Council in 2000. Its chronology also places a sanctions system in 2000, including points, fines and corrective action. Rating a product and policing how companies market it had become related responsibilities. Looking at the dates separately prevents the familiar present-day symbols from being projected backwards as though the whole scheme had arrived fully formed.

old_entry.summary: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is a 1992 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy.
body: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is a 1992 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. It is the sequel to Super Mario Land. In Super Mario Land 2, the player assumes the role of the protagonist Mario, whose main objective is to reclaim his personal island, Mario Land, from the clutches of his greedy rival Wario. The gameplay builds and expands on that of its precursor with innovations carried over from Super Mario World and Super Mario Bros. 3.

Super Mario Land 2 received critical acclaim upon release and sold over 11 million copies, becoming one of the most successful and highest-rated titles on the Game Boy. Reviewers emphasized that the game surpassed its predecessor in all aspects. Super Mario Land 2 marks the debut appearance of Wario, who would become a prominent character in the Super Mario series as the antihero of several games, the first being this game's sequel Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3. Super Mario Land 2 was re-released in 2011 as a downloadable title for the Nintendo 3DS, and the Nintendo Switch in 2023, as part of the Nintendo Classics service.

old_entry.title: Shin Megami Tensei
old_entry.summary: Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom.
body: Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom. Originally released in 1992 in Japan, it has been ported to multiple systems and eventually released in the West for iOS in 2014. It was released on the Virtual Console service in Japan on Wii in 2007 and on Wii U in 2013, as well as the Nintendo Classics service in 2020. It is the third game in the Megami Tensei series and the first in the central Shin Megami Tensei series. The gameplay uses first-person navigation of dungeons and turn-based battles against demons. The player can recruit demons as allies by talking to them rather than fighting them, and two to three demons can be fused to create new demons.

The story follows a player-named protagonist who lives in near-future Tokyo. When a portal to the realm of demons is opened accidentally by a scientist named Steven and is seized by Gotou, a military commander who believes that he can control the demons, the United States government orders a nuclear attack on Tokyo. Transported with two other supporting characters thirty years into the future, the protagonist finds the Earth ruined by a demon invasion, which is now the stage for an escalating conflict between the Order of Messiah and the Ring of Gaia, conflicting cults who wish to bring about kingdoms for their respective patron deities (Yahweh and Lucifer). The story is influenced by moral decisions the protagonist makes, aligning him either with the Messians, the Ring of Gaia, or setting him up as an independent agent.

From the start of the production, Atlus staff saw Shin Megami Tensei as a chance to create a game with the company's brand on it. The staff saw it as a remake of the previous Megami Tensei game; because of this, they knew what was going to happen in the story, and the development went smoothly. The story went through multiple revisions, and many settings were inspired by the staff's personal lives. The character and demon designs were done by Kazuma Kaneko, who used mythical figures and multiple clothing styles in his designs. Critical and commercial reception for the game have been highly positive, and its success helped launch Atlus as a developer and publisher, along with popularizing the Megami Tensei series.

old_entry.title: The Addams Family
old_entry.summary: The Addams Family is a 1992 action-adventure platform game based on the 1991 film of the same name.
body: The Addams Family is a 1992 action-adventure platform game based on the 1991 film of the same name. Developed and published by Ocean Software, it was released for home consoles such as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, computers such as the Amiga, and handheld consoles such as the Game Boy.

The player assumes the role of Gomez Addams. His mission is to rescue other members of the Addams family from the clutches of Abigail Craven, who, alongside The Judge and the family attorney Tully Alford, is attempting to seize the Addams' wealth. The game is non-linear, with the player moving throughout the mansion's many inside and outside areas, some of which are hidden. Enemies include bosses each holding a member of the Addams Family hostage, making them necessary to defeat. Power-ups, extra lives, and money are also obtainable.

Ocean, a leader in the market of video game adaptations of films in the late 1980s, began development of the tie-in for The Addams Family film in April 1991, before the film switched studios from 20th Century Fox to Paramount Pictures. It was originally planned to be a puzzle game for computer consoles until Paramount requested that Ocean develop a version for the SNES. The final result was that all versions, including the computer versions, were platformers with the same storyline, setting and objective. The game was critically well-received for its graphics, sound, and music, but was widely considered to be a derivative platformer of its time.

old_entry.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 2
old_entry.subtitle: Sonic 2 Turns Speed into Collaboration
old_entry.summary: On November 24, 1992, Sonic the Hedgehog 2 arrives on Genesis in North America and Mega Drive in Europe.
body: On November 24, 1992, Sonic the Hedgehog 2 arrives on Genesis in North America and Mega Drive in Europe. Sega records November 21 for Japan, so the November 24 anniversary concerns the Western markets of the 16-bit version. The sequel increases speed, introduces Miles "Tails" Prower and builds broader levels designed to support parallel routes and longer accelerations. The Spin Dash also changes the rhythm: Sonic can build momentum from a standstill and turn a pause into an explosive start. The game adds a competitive split-screen mode and a Special Stage that simulates depth using two-dimensional graphics. Sonic 2 does more than expand the first episode: it clarifies which elements of the series can become system, character and shared spectacle.

In the first Sonic, speed depends mainly on slope, available space and the ability to maintain momentum. Sonic 2 adds the Spin Dash, which lets Sonic crouch, charge a spin and launch quickly even from a stationary position. It is only apparently a small change. Players can recover momentum after a mistake, tackle ramps without searching for a long run-up and turn a pause into a preparatory gesture. The mechanic also reinforces the character's personality: Sonic is not represented as fast only through animation, but gives the player a dedicated command for building speed. The Spin Dash would become one of the series' most recognizable actions because it solves a control problem while making the protagonist's identity more directly playable.

Miles "Tails" Prower enters the series as Sonic's partner and immediately changes the composition of the screen. In the main game he can be controlled by the computer, following the protagonist, collecting rings and attacking enemies, or by a second player with control less constrained by the camera. His ability to return quickly after leaving the frame makes cooperation informal and accessible: the second player can participate without blocking progression. Tails is therefore more than a new mascot. He introduces a particular form of shared play, imperfect but well suited to a platformer built around the main character's speed. Narratively, his presence also defines Sonic by contrast, turning the solitary hero of the first game into someone who can be followed, imitated and accompanied.

To support greater speed, Sonic 2 expands level structure and multiplies routes, elevations and detours. An experienced player can cross some sections while preserving momentum, while someone who slows down finds platforms, enemies and alternate paths that keep the experience under control. This layering prevents speed from becoming an automatic reward: moving fast well requires knowing the terrain, anticipating obstacles and choosing the right trajectory. Zones such as Chemical Plant make the principle obvious, alternating long acceleration stretches with vertical passages, pipes and moments when water imposes a different rhythm. Level design therefore has to reconcile two opposite needs, spectacle and readability. Sonic 2 becomes especially interesting when the run feels spontaneous but is supported by carefully built geography.

Sonic 2's Special Stages abandon the top-down maze of the first game and present a course that appears to extend into depth. Sonic and Tails run through a half-pipe collecting rings and avoiding obstacles, while two-dimensional graphics are scaled and arranged to simulate three-dimensional movement. The effect serves a precise function: it concentrates attention on reaction time and lateral position, temporarily separating the game from the complex geography of normal levels. The technology is not used as a simple visual demonstration, but creates a different and immediately recognizable rule set. Sega itself presents the sequence as a new "3D" Special Stage. In the context of 1992, the choice shows how the Mega Drive can suggest depth through graphic tricks and rhythm without changing the nature of its hardware.

Sonic 2 introduces a competitive two-player split-screen mode. The Mega Drive must draw two views of the same level at once, vertically compressing the image and accepting less elegant readability than the main campaign. In exchange, speed stops being a private sensation and becomes something measured against another person. Reaching the end is not enough: rings, items and overall performance all contribute to the comparison. The mode also shows how well Sonic's language suits local competition, because trajectories and risks can be read in real time by both players. The technical compromise is obvious, but that is precisely what makes it interesting: the image is distorted in order to enable a social relationship that the first game did not offer in the same way.

November 24, 1992 is remembered in Western markets as the launch day of Sonic the Hedgehog 2. Concentrating the Genesis and Mega Drive release on the same day helps Sega turn the sequel into a recognizable event, supported by Sonic's growing importance to the company's identity. It is important, however, to separate communication from the historical record: the 16-bit version had already been released in Japan on November 21, while versions for 8-bit hardware follow different chronologies. This distinction makes the strategy easier to read. Sonic 2 is both a global product and a launch adapted to different markets. The Western anniversary shows how, in the early 1990s, the calendar itself could become a tool for building anticipation around a video game.

old_entry.title: Final Fantasy V
old_entry.summary: Final Fantasy V is a 1992 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Super Famicom.
body: Final Fantasy V is a 1992 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Super Famicom. It is the fifth main installment of the Final Fantasy series. The game begins as a wanderer named Bartz investigates a fallen meteor. There, he encounters several characters, one of whom reveals the danger facing the four Crystals that control the world's elements. These Crystals act as a seal on Exdeath, an evil sorcerer. Bartz and his party must keep the Crystals from being exploited by Exdeath's influence and prevent his resurgence.

It has been ported with minor differences to Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Game Boy Advance. An original video animation produced in 1994 called Final Fantasy: Legend of the Crystals serves as a sequel to the events depicted in the game. It was released for the PlayStation Network on April 6, 2011, in Japan. An enhanced port of the game, with new high-resolution graphics and a touch-based interface, was released for iPhone and iPad on March 28, 2013, for Android on September 25 the same year and for Windows on September 24, 2015. A more enhanced re-release of the game as part of the Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster series, was released on November 10, 2021 for Android, iOS, and Windows, for Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 on April 19, 2023, and for Xbox Series X/S on September 26, 2024.

Final Fantasy V has been praised for the freedom of customization that the player has over the characters, achieved through the greatly expanded Job System. Despite being released only in Japan at the time, the Super Famicom version sold more than two million copies. The PlayStation version has earned "Greatest Hits" status, selling more than 350,000 copies.

body: Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting, released as Street Fighter II Dash Turbo in Japan, is a 1992 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the third arcade version of Street Fighter II, part of the Street Fighter franchise, following Street Fighter II: Champion Edition, and was initially released as an enhancement kit for that game. Released less than a year after the previous installment, Hyper Fighting introduced a faster playing speed and new special moves for certain characters, as well as further refinement to the character balance.

Hyper Fighting is the final arcade game in the Street Fighter II series to use the original CP System hardware. It was distributed as an upgrade kit designed to be installed into Champion Edition printed circuit boards. The next game, Super Street Fighter II, uses the CP System's successor, the CP System II.
